The Present Simple, Simple Past Tenses and Present Continuous Tense

Simple, direct language is used when writing a short report, so simple tenses are mostly used. The situation is described using the Present Simple Tense, and background to the situation is described using the Simple Past Tense. A few critical sentences using the Present Continuous Tense may describe what is currently in process or what main characters are doing about the situation.

The opening sentence in a report about a current situation may use the Present Simple Tense to describe a situation happening at a general or indefinite time period:
Example: A tornado hits Oklahoma again!
City council members approve the subway plan!

The opening sentence may also use the Present Continuous to make the situation feel more real in the moment:
Example: A Tornado is hitting our city!
City council members are approving the subway plan!

General information is given in the Present Simple tense:
Example: Tornadoes are common in this part of the country but they rarely hit the city. This one is bigger than usual and the city is in its direct path.
Example: City residents urgently want a new subway system. Traffic is much too congested in our city. However, the plan is expensive.

Key background information is used with sentences in the Simple Past to fill in context for readers:
Example: Last year we had several tornado warnings but not one impacted the city. The city developed a new plan for emergency evacuation. Children even practiced tornado drills in school.
Example: In August, city council was dead-set against beginning the new subway plans. Members claimed it was too expensive for the city budget.

A closing line may end the piece in the Present Continuous to inform the reader of the current situation or what key actors are doing about it.
Example: Emergency crews are presently preparing in case there is a need for evacuation.

Example: City council is now planning when the excavation can begin.
(Look for the '-ing' to identify the continuous tense!)
A press release is always given in order to leave the public with a general impression that is important to whoever is being represented. Wording must be carefully chosen to convey this feeling.

Often a press release is written to address a situation that people feel strongly about. Emotional language is used to bring the public into the same mood as the writer. Sometimes the situation has a moral or ethical side to it. Word choice will reflect this.

images.text: Holly's Wear and Polygon Ready to Confront Human Rights Issues in Tindasia

Deeply disturbed by rumors that Toronto's Holly's Wear production plant in Shalopolis, Tindasia uses child labor,  William Farmani (CEO) and Janet Ellis (president of Polygon) are joining forces to overturn human rights abuses and bring community change. Holly's Wear is not the only factory using child labor on the island. Impoverished family members of all ages look to foreign and local companies to employ them and bring rice to their tables. In fact, reputable factories that meet worker safety codes, like Holly's, are workplaces of choice for many.

However, Farmani says, “although legal in Tindasia, this is not acceptable business practice. We must bring positive changes to society rather than finding ourselves complicit in exploitation. These children should be preparing for their futures in school.”

“Shocking! It is an outrage! Believe me, I had no idea!”
This was Farmani's reaction when Polygon confronted him with the news they had just learned about the company's human rights concerns. After discovering a rumor through social media, they did a private investigation. Although no crime was found, the company was very upset. The family of one member of management at Polygon has been involved in community relief to the area for several generations. Together, Polygon and Holly's Wear are planning ways to bring better job security to adults that will benefit entire families and keep children in school.
